**Visual Analysis:**

- **Affected plant**: Entire tomato plant (center of frame)
- **Key features**:
  - Complete, sudden collapse of the whole plant — all stems and leaves drooping severely downward
  - Foliage still appears green (no yellowing or necrosis), yet completely wilted
  - Neighboring plants on both sides look healthy and upright
  - Black plastic mulch used (commercial production setting in what appears to be a warm/hot climate)
  - No visible white mycelium at soil line (rules out Southern Blight/Sclerotinia)
  - No visible lesions or spots on leaves (rules out foliar diseases)

**Reasoning:**

The sudden, complete, whole-plant wilt with leaves remaining green is the hallmark of **vascular wilt** caused by a soilborne pathogen blocking water transport. The pattern — single plant collapsing while immediate neighbors are unaffected — is classic. The absence of white fungal growth at the stem base rules out Southern Blight and Sclerotinia. The absence of leaf spotting rules out foliar diseases. Verticillium and Fusarium wilts tend to cause gradual, progressive yellowing rather than this sudden green-but-wilted collapse. The rapid, complete wilt in a warm-climate commercial tomato field on plastic mulch is most consistent with **Bacterial Wilt** (*Ralstonia solanacearum*), which causes irreversible, rapid whole-plant collapse with vascular browning internally.
